# AGENTS.md

## Documentation

The docs are split by audience. Keep each fact in one place.

- `README.md` is for people trying the plugin for the first time. It covers what
  the plugin is, why to use it, and how to install it from scratch. Use short
  sentences and short paragraphs. No limits, file paths, tool names, or
  internals: link to `docs/` instead.
- `docs/guide.md` is the user reference: every feature, its limits, data
  locations, backups, and troubleshooting.
- `docs/architecture.md` covers how the plugin, web app, tunnel, and Desktop
  page fit together, the source layout, and the security model.
- `docs/development.md` covers setup, scripts, reloading, and release rules.

Update the docs in the same change as the code:

- A new or changed feature, limit, setting, or UI label: update
  `docs/guide.md`. Touch `README.md` only if the headline features or the
  install steps change.
- A new file under `plugin/src` or `web/src`, or a changed process, port,
  route, cookie, or secret: update `docs/architecture.md`.
- A new or changed `package.json` script or build step: update
  `docs/development.md`.
- A change to the install steps or requirements: update `install.sh`,
  `README.md`, and `docs/guide.md` together.

## Releases

`dist/` is committed. Run `bun run bundle` and commit `dist/` with every source
change.

# Bots for OpenCode **AI teammates that remember you, and live in your pocket.**
--- Create bots with names, roles, and memory. Put them in group chats. Message them from your phone, and get a notification when the work is done. Everything runs on your own computer. No server, no account, no extra bill. ## What you get - **Bots that remember.** Each bot keeps what you've told it, across every chat. Ask what you talked about weeks ago, and it looks it up. - **Bots with a job.** A reviewer, a researcher, an ops lead. You set the role. - **Bots that team up.** Mention `@someone` and bots pass work to each other. - **Group chats.** One bot hosts, the others jump in when called. - **Bots that follow up.** Each bot keeps a to-do list and sets itself reminders. Ask for a morning briefing and it shows up every morning. - **Bots that open projects.** A bot can start a real OpenCode session in any of your projects, with that project's own agents and skills. It stays in Desktop, so you can check it and pick up where the bot left off. - **Your phone.** A fast chat app, with push notifications. - **Bots that learn.** They suggest new skills after a job well done. You approve. - **Real power.** Every bot is a full OpenCode agent. It can read, write, and run code on your machine. ## New to OpenCode? [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) is a free, open source AI agent. It runs on your computer and can work on your files. It comes with free models, so you can start without an API key. You can also connect OpenAI, Anthropic, GitHub Copilot, and many others. Bots for OpenCode is a plugin. It turns OpenCode into a team you can chat with. ## Install You need a Mac or a Linux computer. **1. Get OpenCode Desktop.** Download it from [opencode.ai/download](https://opencode.ai/download) and open it once. **2. Install the plugin.** Paste this into a terminal: ```sh curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/alefunion/opencode-bots/main/install.sh | bash ``` It installs the OpenCode command line if you don't have it, then adds the plugin. Already use OpenCode? This does the same thing: ```sh opencode plugin add github:alefunion/opencode-bots ``` **3. Pair your phone.** In OpenCode Desktop, open **Settings → Bots**. Click **Pair device** and scan the QR code. **4. Say hi.** Your first bot is **Chief**. Ask it to create more bots for you. > [!TIP] > On your phone, use **Add to Home Screen**. The app opens full screen, and > notifications work there. ## Safe by design The app only listens on your own computer. Your phone reaches it through an encrypted private tunnel. Only devices you pair can get in. Lost your phone? Click **Sign out all devices** in **Settings → Bots**. A paired device can do anything OpenCode can, so pair only devices you own. ## Learn more - [User guide](docs/guide.md): every feature, backups, and troubleshooting. - [Architecture and security](docs/architecture.md): how it works under the hood. - [Development](docs/development.md): build and hack on the plugin. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) OpenCode is a trademark of Anomaly. Bots for OpenCode is an independent project, not made, affiliated with, or endorsed by Anomaly.

# Architecture and security

How Bots for OpenCode runs, and how it keeps your machine private.

## How it runs

```text
Phone / browser
  │  https://bots.<hostname>   (OpenTunnel)
  ▼
Web app  127.0.0.1:49384       prebuilt; serves the UI, proxies /api, sends Web Push
  │
  ▼
OpenCode background service    the one Desktop uses
  ├─ plugin, every location:   keeps one web app process running
  ├─ plugin, bot workspace:    bot tools, persona and memory, library, scheduler, RPC
  └─ Desktop GUI:              Settings → Bots
```

The web app ships prebuilt and runs on the Bun runtime inside OpenCode, so there
is nothing else to install. It is a child of the OpenCode service and is
restarted within seconds if it exits. It finds the service on its own and needs
no password. Plugin instances in other locations do nothing else, so classic
sessions get no bot persona.

OpenCode unloads a location after an hour without session activity, disposing
its plugin instance; the web app stops when the last instance releases it. So
every instance makes sure the bot workspace's `.opencode/opencode.json` sets
`experimental.location_idle_timeout: false` (unless the user set a value), and
the bot workspace, its scheduler, and the web app stay up while idle.

The bot-workspace plugin runs the task and job schedule itself, checking every
20 seconds; OpenCode's native schedules are off by default and not exposed to
plugins. A due job or task wakes its bot with a synthetic message in the bot's
own session (`delivery: "queue"`, `resume: true`), tagged `botsJob` or
`botsTask` in its metadata. That tag is how the app draws the collapsible note,
how notifications are titled, and how `bots_send` treats the scheduled prompt
as the current message. Each run is saved to `bots.json` before the bot is
woken, so a restart can't fire it twice.

Project workers are ordinary top-level sessions, not child sessions. `bots_worker`
calls `session.create` with only a title, `location: { directory }`, and an
optional agent: no `parentID`, model, or permissions. The session therefore
belongs to the target location, which loads that project's own config,
`AGENTS.md`, agents, skills, and MCP servers. The bot-workspace plugin instance
only knows the session by ID: it prompts it (`delivery: "queue"`), waits on it,
reads its context, and interrupts or removes it, and its persona and library
hooks never match it. The plugin instance in the worker's location does nothing
beyond the web host, as in any other location. `bots.json` keeps only the index
(`workers`: ID, owner bot, session ID, directory, title); deleting a bot drops
its entries but leaves the sessions.

`bots_history` reads conversations from OpenCode's own database and keeps no
copy or index. The plugin's `session.context` returns only what follows the
latest compaction, so the plugin finds the background service the way the web
app does (`Service.discover`, with its credentials) and pages through the
service's `message.list` (200 per page, oldest first). Only user, bot, and
synthetic text is kept; a user message with `fromBot` metadata is labelled as
another bot's. Search is a case- and accent-insensitive term match in memory,
ranked by terms matched, then recency. Output is capped: 8 excerpts of about
300 characters per search, and 13 messages of up to 1,200 characters (8,000 in
all) per read. If the service can't be reached, the tool falls back to
`session.context` and says so.

A search from the bot's current chat stops before the message that started the
run, so the question can't match itself. That message is the first user,
bot-to-bot, job, or task message from one second before the session turned
busy on: the service stores it a few milliseconds after `time.busy`, and a bot
message queued later must not move the cut.

**Clear conversation** interrupts the session and archives it
(`session.update`, `archived: true`), retitled and tagged
`botsClearedBot: <bot id>` in its metadata. The tool lists the bot workspace's
sessions, archived and not (a user may unarchive one), and keeps those with the
bot's tag. Their messages are cached for the process, keyed by the session's
last update, least recently used first, up to 20 million characters; a session
that is busy when read is not cached, so a half-written reply never sticks.
Deleting a bot removes those sessions and their cache entries. Nothing new goes
into `bots.json`. Unlike deleting, archiving may leave the old session's
background shells or subagents running, and one that finishes can wake that
session.

Questions and permission prompts are listed per location, so the web app asks
the bot workspace and every unique worker directory (`form.list`,
`permission.request.list`, settled independently and deduplicated by ID and
session), then shows a worker's requests in its owner bot's chat. Answers go by
session ID, which works from any location. For notifications the bot-workspace
plugin subscribes to the global `form.created` and `permission.asked` events and
pushes those whose session is a worker to `/?bot=<owner>`; bot and group
questions are left to the `question` tool hook, so nothing is sent twice.

Dictation borrows the running Hex app instead of loading a speech model of its
own. The web app reads Hex's owner-only discovery file
(`~/Library/Application Support/hex/local-api.json`, `~/.local/share/hex` on
Linux, `HEX_APPLICATION_SUPPORT_DIR` overrides; local API version 2 only) and
relays the browser's audio to Hex's local API:

```text
browser (AudioWorklet → 16 kHz s16le)       web app                 Hex
POST /api/dictation                    →    POST /streams           opens a stream on dictation's model
POST /api/dictation/:id/audio  (¼ s)   →    /streams/{id}/audio
GET  /api/dictation/:id/events (SSE)   ←    /streams/{id}/events    segments and partials, shown live
POST /api/dictation/:id/finish         →    /streams/{id}/finish    final text
POST /api/transcribe  (whole WAV)      →    POST /transcriptions    fallback, model from POST /control
```

The `:id` is the web app's own random id; Hex's stream id and owner token stay
in the web app. The browser keeps every sample, so when Hex can't stream (one
stream at a time) or a stream breaks, it sends the whole clip as a WAV instead.
`GET /api/transcribe` reports whether Hex is installed and answering, which
decides whether the composer shows the microphone.

Both `/streams/{id}/finish` and `/transcriptions` are sent with
`process=global`, which asks for Hex's Global-mode Output processing (Labs ›
Process API transcripts); its `processed` field is used when present. Hex
refuses the parameter before reading the audio or finishing the stream
(`403 processing-disabled`, `409 processing-unavailable`, `429 queue-full`), so
on those codes the web app sends the request again without it and uses the
raw text.

The tunnel reuses the OpenTunnel identity OpenCode itself pairs with (profile
`default`) and claims its own `bots` route, so the address is stable across
restarts. If the profile has no identity yet, the first connect creates one
(`tunnel.ensure`), so nobody has to run `opencode pair --remote` first. OpenCode
then uses the same identity if remote pairing is turned on later.

Requirements: OpenCode Desktop 2.2 or later on macOS or Linux (Windows is not
supported), and port `49384` free on `127.0.0.1`.

## Source layout

```text
plugin/src/index.ts     server plugin: store, hooks, bots_* tools, scheduler, RPC
plugin/src/rpc.ts       RPC contract shared with the web app and Desktop page
plugin/src/schedule.ts  cron and wake-time parsing, shared with the web app
plugin/src/history.ts   bots_history: full session history from the service, search, read
plugin/src/webhost.ts   runs the web app on OpenCode's Bun runtime
plugin/src/gui.tsx      Desktop Settings → Bots page
web/src/index.ts        web app server: pairing, proxy, push, tunnel
web/src/remote.ts       tunnel connection and pairing cookies
web/src/hex.ts          dictation: relays audio to the running Hex's local API
web/src/dictation.ts    browser microphone capture, live streaming, WAV fallback
web/src/face.ts         bot faces drawn as SVG from a saved 8-hex-digit seed
web/src/App.tsx         React app
web/src/components/     chat, sidebar, and Settings tabs (Planner.tsx: Tasks and Jobs;
                        Requests.tsx: question and permission cards)
web/src/sw.js           service worker (push, notification clicks)
```

## Security

- The web app listens on `127.0.0.1` only; remote access is through OpenTunnel.
- Every request needs a pairing cookie, loopback included: the tunnel forwards
  the visitor's `Host` header, so a local-looking request proves nothing.
- Pairing uses OpenCode's single-use codes. The app checks a code with OpenCode
  and issues its own signed cookie (`HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Secure`,
  400 days); OpenCode's session cookie never reaches the browser.
- Cross-origin writes are rejected.
- The plugin's notify requests are authorized by a 256-bit internal secret in
  `push.json` (mode `0600`), not by a local-only check.
- `bots.json` holds roles and memory, not provider credentials.
- `bots_history` answers only for the calling bot's own chat and cleared
  conversations; only the coordinator can name another bot. Group chats are
  never searched.
- Hex's bearer token and stream owner tokens stay in the web app; the browser
  only reaches `/api/dictation` and `/api/transcribe`, behind the pairing cookie
  and origin check like every `/api` route. Audio is held in memory (whole
  clips capped at 24 MB, stream chunks at 256 KiB) and never written to disk.

> [!WARNING]
> A paired device has full use of your OpenCode service, as Desktop does:
> sessions, tools, and shell. Pair only devices you control, and use **Sign out
> all devices** if one is lost.

# Development

## Setup

Clone the repository into OpenCode's global plugin directory, where it is
discovered without a `plugins` entry (don't also install it with
`opencode plugin add`):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/alefunion/opencode-bots ~/.config/opencode/plugins/opencode-bots
cd ~/.config/opencode/plugins/opencode-bots
bun install
bun run bundle
```

## Scripts

```sh
bun run typecheck   # plugin and web app
bun run fmt         # Bun's formatter (settings in bunfig.toml); fmt:check for CI
bun run bundle      # dist/web (web app) and dist/gui-experimental.cjs (Desktop page)
bun run watch:gui   # rebuild the Desktop page while editing it
```

## Reloading

The plugin always runs the prebuilt `dist/web`, so run `bun run bundle` after
changing `web/src`, then reload the plugin (`touch plugin/src/index.ts`); it
replaces the running web app when the bundle changed. Changes to `package.json`
need `opencode service restart`.

`bun run dev` serves `web/src` directly with hot reload. Give it its own port
(`PORT=8890 bun run dev`) and set `BOT_NO_AUTH=1` to skip pairing. It also
claims the `bots` tunnel route while running.

## Committing `dist/`

`dist/` is committed so that installing from Git needs no build step: run
`bun run bundle` and commit `dist/` with every source change. Git installs never
build, and a `build` script would make npm try to compile the package from
source.

## Logo and icons

The logo is drawn on a 16 × 20 grid; see [`public/logo.md`](../public/logo.md).
After changing a mark or the app icon in `public/`, run
`scripts/build-icons.sh`: it compresses the SVGs with SVGO (settings in
`scripts/svgo.config.mjs`) and renders the favicon and Home Screen PNGs. It needs librsvg (`brew install librsvg`).

## Install script

[`install.sh`](../install.sh) is what the README's one-line install runs. It
finds or installs the OpenCode CLI, adds the plugin, and checks for OpenCode
Desktop. It must run on both macOS and Linux, including when piped from `curl`.

# User guide

Everything Bots for OpenCode does, feature by feature. For setup, see the
[README](../README.md).

Requirements: OpenCode Desktop 2.2 or later on macOS or Linux (Windows is not
supported), and port `49384` free on `127.0.0.1`.

## Bots

Each bot is one long-lived OpenCode session with a name, an `@handle`, a role, a
face, and its own memory. Bot sessions live in `~/Bots for OpenCode`,
so you can open them in Desktop too.

- **Names and handles.** Only the name is editable; the handle is derived from it
  (`Research Lead` → `@research-lead`, with a numeric suffix if taken), so
  renaming changes the handle.
- **Face.** A flat shape with two eyes, in a random colour from the iOS system
  palette. In **Settings → Bots**, click **Random face** until you like one, then
  save. Bots created by Chief, and bots from before faces existed, get one
  automatically. Groups keep a coloured square with their initials.
- **Model.** One model for every bot and group, chosen in **Settings → Bots**. A
  session switched to another model elsewhere is switched back on its next
  message.
- **Memory.** Private to each bot. Edit it in **Settings**, or ask the bot to
  remember or forget something (`bots_memory`). Bots save only facts and durable
  preferences you actually stated, never their own guesses, and update an entry
  rather than adding a near-duplicate. Capped at 50 entries and 40,000
  characters.
- **Role.** The bot's standing instructions. Edit it in **Settings**, or ask the
  bot to change it (`bots_role`). Bots change their role only when you ask, and
  only their own; the new role applies from the next model step. Write only the
  role body: the name, `@handle`, and `Role` heading are added to the system
  prompt automatically, so don't repeat them in the field.
- **Conversation history.** Long chats are compacted: the bot keeps working
  from a summary of older messages, so details drop out of what it sees. Ask
  about something you said before ("what was that library I mentioned last
  week?") and the bot searches its past messages word for word
  (`bots_history`), then answers from what it finds, or says it found nothing.
  It sees short excerpts of the best matches (up to 8), can narrow them by date,
  and reads the messages around one to scroll back or forward, so a search
  never fills its context. It searches only its own chat, cleared
  conversations included, not group chats; the coordinator can also search
  another bot's history. History is read from OpenCode's database; nothing is
  copied. Your messages, the bot's replies, other bots' messages to it, and
  automatic messages are searched; tool calls and their output are not.
- **Clear conversation.** In **Settings → Bots**, **Clear conversation** stops a
  running reply and starts a fresh session. The old session is archived, not
  deleted: it appears in Desktop's archived sessions as "Name (cleared date)",
  and the bot can still search it until the bot is deleted, even if you
  unarchive it. Work the old session had running in the background, such as a
  long shell command, may keep running. Role, memory, tasks,
  jobs, commands, skills, and project workers are kept. Group chats and worker
  sessions are separate and are not cleared.
- **Coordinator.** Only the coordinator can create bots (`bots_create`). The
  first bot, **Chief** (`@chief`), starts as the coordinator. Choose another in
  **Settings → Bots**; deleting it clears the setting.
- **Bot-to-bot messages.** Bots reach each other with `@handle`, so one bot can
  delegate to another.
- **Questions and permissions.** When a bot asks you something with OpenCode's
  question tool, or needs a permission you set to ask, it waits until you
  answer. The question appears as a card at the end of the chat, and the chat
  shows **Waiting for your answer** in the sidebar. Pick an option or type your
  own answer, then **Send answer**; **Dismiss** lets the bot carry on without
  one. A group member's questions appear in the group too, and a
  [project worker](#project-workers)'s appear in its bot's chat, labelled with
  the worker and its project. You can also answer in Desktop.
- **Attachments.** Use `+` in the composer (or `Cmd`/`Ctrl` + `U`), paste, or
  drag files in: up to 10 files, 10 MB each, 25 MB in total.
- **Dictation.** With [Hex](https://github.com/anomalyco/hex) running on the
  computer that runs OpenCode, the composer shows a microphone. Tap it, speak,
  then tap the red stop button: the words appear where the cursor was, ready to
  edit and send. `×` or `Escape` discards the recording. It works from your
  phone too, because that computer does the transcribing, on the model and
  language Hex dictates with. The audio goes to Hex while you speak, so the text
  is ready as soon as you stop, and what Hex has heard shows above the text box:
  each phrase once you pause, or word by word with a model that streams. While
  Hex is busy with another stream, the recording is sent whole when you stop
  instead, with no live text; clips over 30 seconds then make Hex load a second
  copy of its model for a while. Recordings stop at 10 minutes and are never
  saved. With **Labs › Process API transcripts** on in Hex (Hex 3.4 or later),
  the text gets your Global mode's Output processing, as a paste would:
  replacements, corrections, rewriting, and transformations. The live text
  shows the words as heard, and the processed text replaces it when you stop.
  With the lab off, or while Hex is processing another request, you get the
  words as heard. The microphone is hidden if Hex has never run on that
  computer.
- **Deleting a bot** deletes its OpenCode session and the sessions of its
  cleared conversations, as in Desktop. If that fails, the bot is kept so no
  session is orphaned. A bot that hosts a group can't be
  deleted until the group has another host. Its project workers' sessions are
  kept in Desktop; only the bot's list of them goes.
- **A session deleted elsewhere** is recreated on the next message. The history
  is gone, so the bot can't search it either; the role and memory still apply.
  The same goes for an archived cleared conversation deleted in Desktop.

## Groups

A group has a host bot, members, and group instructions. The host writes the
replies; mention a member with `@handle` and the host routes the message to it.
Each member's reply appears as its own bubble. Only members can be contacted
from a group.

## Tasks and jobs

See every bot's tasks and jobs in the app's **Settings → Tasks** and
**Settings → Jobs**, filter them by bot, and edit them there; changes apply
immediately.

- **Tasks** are each bot's board: **To do**, **In progress**, and **Done**.
  Bots keep it current with `bots_task` on their own, without being asked:
  whenever they promise to do something later, wait on something outside the
  chat, hear of a deadline, take on multi-step work, or need to check later that
  something worked. Open tasks appear in the bot's instructions, so it always
  knows what's pending.
- **Wake times.** A task can have a wake time. When it arrives, the bot gets a
  task reminder in its own chat and acts on it, then marks the task done or
  snoozes it with a new wake time. Bots accept `45m`, `2h`, `3d`, a local time
  such as `2026-11-09 09:00` (a bare date means 09:00), or an ISO timestamp.
- **Jobs** post a prompt into a bot's chat on a cron schedule (five fields, such
  as `0 9 * * 1-5`, or a macro such as `@daily`), in a time zone that defaults
  to your machine's. Bots create them with `bots_job` when you ask for
  something recurring, and on their own when their role implies a recurring
  duty or you describe a need that keeps coming back. A bot that schedules a job
  itself says so in its reply, runs it at most once a day unless you ask for
  more, and changes or deletes jobs you set up only when you ask. One-off
  follow-ups are tasks with a wake time, not jobs. **Run now** queues a run at
  once; a job can run at most every 5 minutes. Pause a job to keep it without
  running it.
- **The coordinator** sees every bot's open tasks and can assign tasks and
  schedule jobs for any bot; other bots manage only their own.
- **Automatic messages.** Job runs and task reminders appear in the chat as a
  collapsible note, not as your message. They queue behind a reply in progress,
  and a prompt that mentions `@handle` may delegate to that bot.
- **While OpenCode is off**, nothing runs. A job that was due runs once when the
  service is back, marked late; overdue tasks wake their bots at once.
- **Limits.** 50 open tasks per bot, 300 tasks, and 50 jobs. Done tasks are
  removed after 30 days. Deleting a bot deletes its tasks and jobs.

## Project workers

A bot can open a worker: an ordinary OpenCode session in one of your project
directories, created by the bot with `bots_worker`. Ask a bot to "start a
session in `~/code/app` and fix the failing test", and it does the work there.

- **Visible in Desktop.** A worker is a real top-level session in that project,
  not a subagent. It shows up in the project's session list in Desktop and the
  CLI, where you can read it, answer it, and keep going yourself.
- **The project's own setup.** A worker gets that project's `AGENTS.md`,
  agents, commands, skills, MCP servers, permissions, and default model, just
  like a session you start there. It gets none of the bot's role, memory,
  library skills, model, or bot tools, so the bot briefs it in full.
- **Actions.** `create` opens a worker in an existing directory (absolute or
  `~/…`; not the bot workspace), with an optional title, agent from that
  project, and first message. `send` continues it, `read` returns its latest
  reply, `status` shows its title, location, agent, model, and whether it is
  working, `interrupt` stops its current run, `list` shows the bot's workers,
  and `delete` removes it.
- **Long work.** With a message, the bot waits up to 2 minutes for the reply.
  Longer work keeps running; the bot checks back with `read` or `status`, or
  sends with `wait: false` and moves on. Replies over 12,000 characters are cut
  short in the bot's chat; the full text is in the session.
- **Questions and permissions.** When a worker asks something or needs a
  permission, the card appears in its bot's chat (and any group the bot is in),
  labelled with the worker and its project, and the chat shows **Waiting for
  your answer**. You get a notification that opens the bot's chat, so you can
  answer from your phone.
- **Who manages what.** A bot manages only its own workers; the coordinator
  manages everyone's. In a group, the host's workers belong to the host.
- **Deleting.** Bots delete a worker only when you ask, and `delete` removes the
  session and its history. Deleting a bot keeps its workers' sessions in
  Desktop.
- **Limits.** 25 workers per bot, 100 in total. Titles up to 200 characters,
  messages up to 20,000.

## Commands and skills

Manage both in the app's **Settings**, or ask a bot to create them.

- **Commands** are prompt templates: type `/name` in a chat. Templates support
  `$ARGUMENTS` and `$1`…`$9`; without a placeholder, the arguments are appended.
- **Skills** are directories in `~/.local/share/opencode/bots/skills/<id>/`: a
  `SKILL.md` plus any references, scripts, or assets. Bots load them with
  OpenCode's skill tool, by description or `@skill-id`. Add files or whole
  folders in **Settings → Skills**; scripts under `scripts/` are made
  executable. Limits: 4 MB per file, 200 files and 40 MB per skill. A skill ID
  can't change after the first save.
- **Scope.** Each item is available to **All bots** or **Selected bots**. Items a
  bot creates are scoped to that bot, but any bot can edit or delete any library
  item, shared ones included.
- **Draft proposals.** After a task whose success something outside the bot
  confirmed (tests passed, you said it worked), a bot can propose a skill with
  `bots_skill` action `propose` and the evidence. Proposals arrive in
  **Settings → Skills** as drafts and can't be used until you approve them. Bots
  prefer a minimal `patch` to an existing skill over a rewrite, and `save` only
  when you ask for a new or changed skill.
- **Pinning.** Pin a skill to lock it: bots can no longer save, patch, delete, or
  edit its files. Unpin it to hand it back.
- **Usage and archiving.** **Settings → Skills** shows how often and when each
  skill was loaded. Bot-authored, unpinned skills unused for 60 days are archived
  automatically; they stay in the Library and can be restored, but bots can't
  load them. Skills you create and pinned skills are never archived.
- **Isolation.** Library items exist only in bot and group sessions. Classic
  OpenCode sessions never see them, and bots still have every global OpenCode
  skill.

## Pairing devices

Open **OpenCode Desktop → Settings → Bots**, click **Pair device**, and scan the
QR code (or open the link on another computer). Links work once and expire after
five minutes; the pairing itself is permanent.

The app lives at `https://bots.<your-opentunnel-hostname>`, shown on the same
settings page.

## Notifications

In the app, open **Settings → Remote → Notifications** and tap **Enable
notifications**. Each device opts in separately; **Send test** checks delivery.

- You're notified when a bot or group you messaged finishes, and when a job run
  or task reminder does (each job can turn this off), and when a bot asks you
  a question (including from a job or another bot) or one of its project
  workers asks a question or needs a permission. Bot-to-bot and
  group-member replies stay quiet, background work is allowed to finish first,
  and failed runs don't notify. Tapping a notification opens the conversation.
- It's standard Web Push with keys generated on your machine: no Apple Developer
  account, APNs certificate, or third-party push service.
- **iPhone and iPad** need iOS 16.4 or later. Add the app to the Home Screen,
  open it from the icon, and pair and enable notifications there; a Safari tab
  can't subscribe. Removing the icon removes its subscription.

## Signing devices out

**OpenCode Desktop → Settings → Bots → Sign out all devices** rotates the pairing
secret. Every paired phone and computer is signed out and stops receiving
notifications; the address stays the same, so new pairing links work at once.
Deleting `~/.local/share/opencode/bots/remote.json` does the same. Revocation is
all-or-nothing: there is no per-device sign-out.

## Updating and removing

```sh
opencode plugin update opencode-bots
opencode plugin add github:alefunion/opencode-bots#<tag>   # pin a release
opencode plugin remove opencode-bots
```

## Data and backups

```text
~/Bots for OpenCode/                    bot and group sessions' location
└── .opencode/opencode.json             keeps the location loaded while idle
~/.local/share/opencode/bots/
├── bots.json      bots, groups, model, memory, commands, skill index, tasks, jobs, worker index, coordinator
├── skills/        skill directories
├── remote.json    tunnel hostname + pairing secret (0600)
├── push.json      Web Push keys, internal notify secret, subscriptions (0600)
└── web.log        web app log (0600)
```

`$XDG_DATA_HOME` replaces `~/.local/share` when set. Installs from before the
rename keep using `~/OpenCode Bots`, because their bot sessions belong to it.
Conversations themselves, project workers' sessions included, are in OpenCode's
database, `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db`; `bots.json` only records which
sessions are whose workers. A cleared conversation's session is tagged with its
bot in OpenCode's own session metadata, and is found in the bot sessions'
location: moved elsewhere, it is no longer searched or deleted with the bot.

To back up, copy the whole `bots/` directory; `bots.json` alone doesn't include
skill files. Without `remote.json` every device must pair again; without
`push.json` devices resubscribe on their next open. Back up `opencode.db` too
(with `sqlite3 … ".backup …"`) to keep history, since `bots.json` refers to its
sessions.

## Troubleshooting

**The app is unreachable.** Check that the web app is listening, then read its
log and OpenCode's:

```sh
lsof -nP -iTCP@127.0.0.1:49384 -sTCP:LISTEN
tail -50 ~/.local/share/opencode/bots/web.log
tail -100 ~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log
```

The web app needs port `49384` free on `127.0.0.1`.

**The app goes unreachable after a while idle.** OpenCode unloads a location
after an hour without session activity, and the web app stops once every
location is unloaded. The plugin sets `experimental.location_idle_timeout` to
`false` in `~/Bots for OpenCode/.opencode/opencode.json` so the bot workspace
stays loaded, which also keeps tasks and jobs firing. It leaves the setting
alone if you already chose a value there; delete the key to get the default
back.

**Dictation says Hex isn't running.** Open Hex on the computer that runs
OpenCode (`hex start`) and finish its setup, so its model is downloaded;
`hex status` should list the model as installed. If the browser says microphone access is blocked, allow it
for the app's address in the browser's site settings.

**The address never appears in Settings → Bots.** On first start the app
creates its tunnel address, which needs a connection to `opentunnel.xyz`. Check
`web.log` for the error.

# Bots for OpenCode — icon notes

The mark is a small robot face in a thick frame: two eyes over a shaded band, inside a window cut into a solid block.

- **Grid.** 16 × 20 units. The frame is 4 units thick, the window 8 × 12, each eye 2 × 4, and the shaded band fills the lower 8 units of the window.
- **Tones.** Light backgrounds: `#000000` mark, shade in the same black at 17.6% opacity (`#D2D2D2` on white). Dark backgrounds: `#FFFFFF` mark, shade in the same white at 29.4% opacity (`#4B4B4B` on black). Keep three decimals so the shade lands exactly on those greys.
- **Whole pixels.** Scale in whole steps (16 × 20px, 32 × 40px, …) so every edge lands on a pixel: 32 × 40px in the app. Smallest legible size: 16 × 20px. The favicon centres the mark on a 20 × 20 square.
- **App icon.** Measured from OpenCode's own iOS app icon (`packages/desktop/icons/prod/ios/AppIcon-512@2x.png` in anomalyco/opencode, which its web app serves as the apple-touch-icon), on the same 1024 canvas:
  - Mark at x 231–791, y 162–862: 16 × 20 units of 35px, so the window interior is 280 × 420 at (371, 302), exactly where OpenCode's is.
  - Background: a full square with a vertical gradient, `#343434` to `#181818`. No rounded corners: iOS and Android apply their own mask.
  - Frame: lit from above, `#FFFFFF` to `#B2B2B2`.
  - Shadow: a black rectangle 10px wider on each side and 48px longer below than the frame, blurred 7px across and 28px down.
  - Window: a dark well (`#010101` to `#292929`) above one shaded square, the mark's 8 × 8 grey band, `#525250` turning olive `#1E1808` at the bottom, with darker side walls. OpenCode's ledge and inset band are left out, so it reads as a single square as in the flat mark.
  - Eyes: the frame's material and lighting at their own size, with a small shadow below.
  - No edge highlights or bevel lines on any shape: on the Home Screen, iOS draws its own. OpenCode's grain texture is left out too: it disappears at Home Screen sizes.
  - The same file serves as the maskable icon, as OpenCode's does.
- Outside the app icon, flat geometry only: no colour, gradients, drop shadows, glows, or outlines. No lettering, and no OpenCode O-frame or wordmark, so it does not suggest Anomaly made or endorses it.

Files: `mark-light.svg` (dark mark for light backgrounds), `mark-dark.svg` (light mark for dark backgrounds), `mark.svg` (switches with the system theme, source of the favicon), `logo.svg` (1024px app icon, drawn by hand). `scripts/build-icons.sh` compresses the SVGs with SVGO and renders the favicon and the PNGs.
